# DR-062 · The branch nominates the Job, the trailer nominates the Actor, and the squash carries both

*2026-09-03*

DR-060 said ownership is recovered by asking GitHub, and implemented it as
"list the pull requests this account authored". That is vacuous here:
a solorepo is one solo, so authorship is constant and the question — which
pull request is *this thread* answerable for — was never asked.

**The branch is where the Job already is.** One branch, one pull request,
by construction. It is what an agent wakes up on, it is in `gh pr list`
at no extra cost, and it never touches the permanent subject line. The
ontology already says a Job answers exactly one Challenge — every hop from
Job to Challenge is single-valued, which is the path `check.py` walks for
Collaboration membership — so "one thread, one pull request" is that
constraint met rather than a new rule.

It is one-way, and the direction matters for the Collaboration mission: a
Job has one Challenge, a Challenge has many Jobs. Two agents on one pull
request stays legal. One thread across two pull requests is what has no
meaning, because on restart "which do I resume" would have no answer.

**The trailer says who, not which.** A restart is a new Execution of the
same Job (DR-004), so keying on the workload identity is exactly wrong —
it is the thing that changes. What persists is the Job, and the branch
names it. The trailer names the Actor that took it, which nothing else
records once the session is gone.

**And the squash had to be looked at, because it decides what survives.**
Under `PR_BODY` every trailer was discarded at merge and the pull request
body was duplicated into the commit. Both are wrong in the same direction:
the body is already durable as the pull request, and a commit message is a
label. `COMMIT_MESSAGES` keeps the labels, carries the trailers through,
and leaves the reasoning where it was routed.

**Options considered.**

- _Resolve what a thread owns by authorship_ — rejected. Every pull request in a solorepo is the solo's by construction (DR-014), so `--author @me` reconstructs a fact that was never in doubt and answers nothing about which agent is answerable for which change.
- _Resolve by branch, and name the Actor in a commit trailer_ — chosen. One branch is one pull request, so the checkout is already the token and no new field is needed anywhere. The trailer carries what the branch cannot — which thread took the Job — and costs one line per commit. What neither does is say under which Remit, which is the audit question and is deliberately left alone.
- _A Job identifier in the pull request title_ — rejected. The title becomes the permanent subject on `main` under squash, and ownership is transient — it means nothing after the merge. It also spends the index on a token nobody searches for, against PR First's own step.

**Consequences.**

- `squash_merge_commit_message` moves from `PR_BODY` to `COMMIT_MESSAGES`. The body was already durable as the pull request; copying it into the commit made every subject on `main` carry an essay, which is A14 read backwards.
- The Actor trailers now survive the merge, because the squashed body is the branch's commit messages. The durable half of "who did this" is held by a setting rather than by a heading on the form.
- `Co-Authored-By` is retired. It named a co-author who is not a person and told a maintainer nothing.
- The trail from `main` back to the argument still needs GitHub. `(#n)` in the subject is a pointer, and dereferencing it leaves the clone — which is A13's sharper edge (DR-052) and not new here.

**What would falsify this.** A restart in a fresh worktree, where the branch is not checked out and nothing resolves. The branch is the token only while the checkout exists.

**Bearing on the Charter.** Applies A14.

**Supersedes.** [DR-060](DR-060.md)
